title: Three births: the third is death
hookLine: the Aitareya counts a person's births, and gets to three, and the third one is what most people would call dying

lines: HOW MANY BIRTHDAYS DO YOU HAVE?
cards: How many birthdays do you have? One, obviously. It's on your ID.
Ask a family and it gets fuzzier. There's the day you were born. There's the day, months before, when someone found out you were coming.
And in some families there's a day after the person is gone, when the family gathers and the rites send them on. The Aitareya's second chapter counts births too.
It counts three, and it puts them somewhere you might not expect.

teach.h: THE FIRST BIRTH: IN THE FATHER.
teach.b: The first birth, the text says, happens in the father.
The seed is the strength gathered from all his limbs, a self carried in himself. When he places it in the mother, that's the first birth. Then the second.
The child becomes one with the mother, and so, the text says, she doesn't harm it. She nourishes this self inside her, and so she is to be nourished in turn.
The father cares for the child before birth and after, and so the line goes on and the worlds continue. The child's arrival is the second birth. Then the third.
The child grows and takes the parent's place, carrying on the good work. And the parent, having done what there was to do, grows old and departs.
And departing, the text says, he is born again. That's the third birth. Here is a core Hindu teaching in one line: death isn't the opposite of birth.
It's the next one. The self goes on, and the tradition surrounds that crossing with care.
The funeral rite is called antyeshti, the last offering, and in the days and years after, families make shraddha offerings for those who have gone ahead.

Then the chapter turns to a seer, Vamadeva, and quotes his verse from the Rig Veda: while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. A hundred iron fortresses held me down, and like a hawk I broke out.
So when a Hindu family says someone has passed on, they mean on.

how: Hindu life-cycle rites, the samskaras, mark stages from before birth through death, and the funeral rites (antyeshti) and later shraddha offerings are understood by many families as sending the departed on to their next life.

o: the father in whom the first birth happens
the god who carries the dead to their next birth
the seer who knew the gods' births in the womb

games.q: the three births — tap the pairs.
p: the child born from the mother

s: in the Aitareya, death is the third birth
departing, the parent is born again: that's the third birth.
the text says the mother needs no special care
she nourishes the self within her, so she is to be nourished.
the Vamadeva verse is quoted from the Rig Veda
while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods.

games.q: at a Hindu funeral, a friend hears the priest say the rites help the person 'go on.' she whispers: go on where? what fits the Aitareya?
o: nowhere; the rites are only for the family's grief.
departing is the third birth: the self goes on, and the rites see it off.
back into the same body after the mourning days.
games.why: the Aitareya counts three births, and the third is departing: the parent, having done what there was to do, is born again. antyeshti and shraddha send the departed on.

practice: Let one breath go to the people who carried you before you were born, whoever held the hope of you, and one to those who fed and held you before you could thank them.
Then, gently, think of someone who has died; in the Aitareya's count, that was a birth too. Let a breath go to them, wherever they are.

wordCard.voice: Vamadeva, the seer who said, while still in the womb, I knew all the births of the gods. The Aitareya counts three births: conception in the father, birth from the mother, and death, when a person departs and is born again.

orig.note: Sanskrit Vāmadeva: the Rig Veda seer whose womb verse the Aitareya quotes in 2.5.

carryVoice: Take this with you: dying is the third birth. Tomorrow, the Aitareya's last chapter asks who the self is. That's day four hundred three.
